references.text: Jesus uses a similar image of servanthood where the master and servants switch roles—the master ties on his apron and lets the servants sit down to eat. In [ref:Luk 12:37|Luke 12:37], Jesus shows the surprising grace where the master himself serves, while in Luke 17:7 he emphasizes the servant's duty.

The continuation of the parable in [ref:Luk 17:8-10|Luke 17:8-10] expands on the point from verse 7: the servant must first attend to the master's needs, and when everything is done, he should consider himself a "useless servant" who has only done his duty.

In [ref:Matt 24:45-46|Matthew 24:45-46], Jesus speaks of the faithful and wise servant who does his master's will. Both passages deal with servanthood and the expectation of faithful service without demanding reward.

Paul says in [ref:1 Kor 9:16-17|1 Corinthians 9:16-17] that preaching the gospel is a duty entrusted to him, not something to boast about. This reflects the principle in Luke 17:7 that the servant cannot expect special thanks for doing what he was commanded.
In [ref:Luk 15:4|Luke 15:4], Jesus uses a similar rhetorical question—"Which of you"—as an introduction to a parable. It is a typical device in Jesus' teaching to engage his listeners.

Paul asks rhetorically in [ref:Rom 11:35-36|Romans 11:35-36] who has given God anything first, so that God owes him repayment. This underscores the same principle as in Luke 17:7: a person cannot claim God's favor as earned wages.

In [ref:Rom 6:16|Romans 6:16], Paul speaks of being servants (δοῦλοι) who obey their master. The image of the slave (δοῦλος) plowing or shepherding in Luke 17:7 reflects this same understanding of complete submission to the master.
